item.research_question: What is the fundamental mechanism responsible for the loss of ductility with increasing temperature in single-phase face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys, specifically CrMnFeCoNi?
item.material_system: Equiatomic Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 (single-phase) and nonequiatomic Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 (dual-phase with Cr-rich σ)
item.processing_route: Arc melting under argon atmosphere, homogenization at 1200°C for 48 hours, hot rolling at 1100°C to 8 mm, cold rolling to 2.4 mm (70% reduction), annealing at 1000°C for 1 hour (single-phase) or 900°C for 1 hour (dual-phase)
item.test_conditions: Quasi-static tensile tests at 25° to 800°C, strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹, samples held at temperature for ~10 min before testing
key_findings: Ductility loss in single-phase Cr20MnFe20Co20Ni20 occurs at intermediate temperatures (400° to 700°C) with fracture shortly after ultimate tensile stress.
Fracture mode changes from fully ductile transgranular failure at 25°C to mixed brittle intergranular and ductile transgranular failure at 700°C.
Atom probe tomography reveals nanosized regions (~5 nm thickness) at grain boundaries enriched with Cr, Ni, and Mn after testing at 700°C.
No second-phase precipitates were detected along grain boundaries by XRD, TEM, or SEM-EDS after testing at 700°C.
Cr and Ni segregate separately at grain boundaries, while Ni and Mn tend to cosegregate.
The dual-phase Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14 alloy exhibits increased ductility with temperature and no intergranular embrittlement at 600° and 700°C.
Trace elements C and B segregate at grain boundaries but at concentrations (0.2 at% C, 0.008 at% B) insufficient to form carbides or borides.
item.mechanism: Ductility loss is caused by the fast segregation of principal elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) into grain boundaries during deformation at intermediate temperatures, forming nanoclusters that reduce grain boundary cohesion and promote crack initiation. The authors propose that Cr and Ni segregate separately due to repulsion, while Ni and Mn cosegregate, potentially forming brittle phases or reducing cohesion via magnetic contributions. Preexisting Cr-rich σ phases can absorb these embrittling elements, preventing their segregation to grain boundaries.
item.limitations: The study notes that grain refinement in HEAs can assist the segregation of principal elements to grain boundaries and lead to brittle intermetallic phases, making grain refinement ineffective for avoiding this specific embrittlement. Additionally, the dual-phase alloy designed for proof-of-concept has lower ductility than the single-phase alloy below 500°C.
item.future_work: The authors suggest that the ductility of HEAs at intermediate temperatures can be further improved if the morphology, dimension, and distribution of secondary phases are optimized further following the proposed GB segregation engineering strategy.
quotes: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs.
The segregation of elements Cr, Ni, and Mn into GBs in current HEA occurred during tensile tests at 700°C.
We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases.
